1:3.headline: The stumbling blocks of the wicked: their traps, or their fall?
1:3.body: המכשלות are stumbling blocks. Metzudat David says they are the tricks the wicked used to trip others, which will vanish along with them, while Radak says they are troubles the wicked themselves will trip over and die.

sources.quote: התחבולות מה שהרשעים מכשילים בהם את הבריות יאבדו הם עם הרשעים
sources.says: Metzudat David says the schemes the wicked use to trip people will be destroyed along with the wicked.

sources.quote: יצאו לקראתם צרות שיכשלו בהם שימותו
sources.says: Radak says troubles will come out to meet the wicked, and they will stumble on them and die.

1:4.headline: Idol priests in black, and God's priests beside them
1:4.body: כמרים are idol priests. Radak says they wore black for their worship, and Malbim reads the "priests" named beside them as God's own priests, swept away together with the idolaters.

sources.quote: הכמרים הם לובשי שחורים לשם עכו"ם
sources.says: Radak says the כמרים are those who wear black for idol worship, and the כהנים are those who serve the idols.

sources.quote: כן יקראו כהני עבודת כוכבים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says this is the name for priests of idol worship.

sources.quote: הם הכהנים עובדי השמש עם הכהנים כהני ה'. כי יכרית צדיק עם רשע
sources.says: Malbim says the כמרים serve the sun, and the כהנים beside them are God's priests, since the righteous will be cut off with the wicked.

1:7.headline: Not 'made holy' but 'invited': God sets a grim feast
1:7.body: הקדיש usually means made holy. Here, say Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion, it means invited, and Radak says the guests at God's feast are the birds and beasts who will eat the slain.

sources.quote: הקדיש - הכין וזימן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says הקדיש means prepared and invited.

sources.quote: ענין הזמנה כמו קדשו קהל
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means inviting, as in "gather the assembly."

sources.quote: זימן לאותו זבח קראיו והם עוף השמים וחית השדה
sources.says: Radak says God invited guests to this slaughter, the birds of the sky and beasts of the field, to eat the slain.

1:8.headline: What was wrong with 'foreign clothes'?
1:8.body: God will punish all who wear מלבוש נכרי, strange clothing. Rashi says it means idol ornaments, Ibn Ezra proud dress that set officials apart from the people, and Radak's father fine clothes seized from the weak.

sources.quote: תַּכְשִׁיטֵי עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
sources.says: Rashi says it means the ornaments of idol worship.

sources.quote: כנגד כל עם הארץ, דרך גאות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means clothing unlike everyone else's, worn out of pride.

sources.quote: כשהיו רואים לשום אדם שהיה להם כח עליו מלבוש נאה היו גוזלים אותו ממנו ולובשים אותו
sources.says: Radak cites his father: when they saw a nice garment on someone in their power, they robbed it and wore it.

sources.quote: וי"מ אנשים שמראים עצמם פרושים וחסידים ולובשים מלבוש נכרי
sources.says: Radak adds that some explain it as men who pose as pious and wear special dress so people will notice them.

1:9.headline: Those who leap over the threshold
1:9.body: The Targum and Rashi say these people copied the Philistines, whose priests would not step on the threshold of Dagon's temple. Radak's father reads it as servants who rushed into poor men's houses to grab what their masters wanted.

sources.quote: שֶׁלֹּא הָיוּ דּוֹרְכִים עַל מִפְתַּן דָּגוֹן
sources.says: Rashi brings the Targum: they followed the Philistine custom of not stepping on Dagon's threshold.

sources.quote: מצינו שהחמירו ישראל בעכו"ם יותר מאומות העולם
sources.says: Radak cites a midrash that Israel was even stricter about idol worship than the nations, since the Philistine priests only avoided the threshold but Israel leapt over it.

sources.quote: שידלגו על מפתן בית העני מרוב חפזם לקחתו
sources.says: Radak cites his father: they leapt over the poor man's threshold in their hurry to take what they wanted.

1:10.headline: 'The Second': which part of Jerusalem?
1:10.body: המשנה means "the second." Rashi reads it as the Bird Gate, second to the Fish Gate; Metzudat Zion as the quarter between the two walls; and Radak as the house of study.

sources.quote: מִשַּׁעַר הָעוֹפוֹת שֶׁהוּא שֵׁנִי לוֹ
sources.says: Rashi says it is the Bird Gate, which is second to the Fish Gate.

sources.quote: ר״ל בין שתי החומות שהיא משנה לעיר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it is the area between the two walls, a second part of the city.

sources.quote: היא בית המדרש כמו שנאמר בספר מלכים והיא יושבת בירושלים במשנה
sources.says: Radak says it is the house of study, as in "she sat in Jerusalem in the Mishneh," said of the prophetess Huldah.

sources.quote: לוֹד, שֶׁהִיא מִשְׁנֶה לִירוּשָׁלַיִם
sources.says: Rashi brings a midrash that it is Lod, second to Jerusalem.

1:11.headline: 'People of Canaan' means traders
1:11.body: In this verse כנען does not mean the old Canaanites. Radak reads it as merchants, as Hosea says "a trader with false scales in his hand," while the Targum reads it as people whose deeds are like the Canaanites'.

sources.quote: סוחר כמו כנען בידו מאזני מרמה
sources.says: Radak says כנען means a merchant, as in "a trader with false scales in his hand."

sources.quote: דְּדָמֵי עוֹבָדֵיהוֹן לְעוֹבְדֵי עַמָּא דְאַרְעָא דִכְנָעַן
sources.says: Rashi brings the Targum: the people whose deeds resemble those of the people of the land of Canaan.

1:12.headline: People like wine left sitting on its dregs
1:12.body: קפאים pictures wine left still on its sediment. Radak and Malbim read it as thickened and unmoving, people settled comfortably on their wealth, while Rashi reads it as floating on top.

sources.quote: שהם שקטים בבתיהם על ממונם כמו היין שהוא שקט על שמריו
sources.says: Radak says they sit quiet in their houses on their wealth, like wine resting on its dregs.

sources.quote: דבר הנקפא ונגלד עומד על מקום אחד ואינו מתנועע
sources.says: Malbim says it is something that has set and thickened and stays in one place without moving.

sources.quote: הַצָּפִים עַל שִׁמְרֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says it means floating on their dregs, since the Targum renders "the iron floated" with this word.

1:14.headline: Who is screaming: the warrior, or the day itself?
1:14.body: The verse says "bitter, screaming there, a warrior." Rashi and Ibn Ezra say the warrior screams bitterly, while Radak suggests the day of the LORD itself cries out, and that warriors will be killed there.

sources.quote: הַגִּבּוֹר יִצְרַח שָׁם בְּקוֹל מַר
sources.says: Rashi says the warrior will scream there in a bitter voice.

sources.quote: אמר כאלו יום ה' קורא ומגביה קולו וקורא מר
sources.says: Radak says it is as if the day of the LORD itself calls out loudly and bitterly.

sources.quote: תַּמָן גִבָּרַיָא מִתְקַטְלִין
sources.says: The Targum says "there the warriors are killed."

1:17.headline: Not 'their bread' but 'their flesh,' as in Arabic
1:17.body: לחם usually means bread, but this rare form means flesh. Rashi and Ibn Ezra both point to Arabic, where the word for meat is lahm: their bodies will be thrown out like dung.

sources.quote: וּלְשׁוֹן עַרְבִי, בָּשָׂר קוֹרִין
sources.says: Rashi says ולחמם means their flesh, since in Arabic meat is called al-lahm.

sources.quote: בשרם בלשון ישמעאל
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says it means their flesh, in the Arabic language.

sources.quote: כן יקרא גם הבשר
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says flesh is also called by this word.

1:18.headline: A sudden end, or only a scare?
1:18.body: The verse says God will make "an end, only a terror" of everyone in the land. Radak reads it as a sudden destruction, while Malbim hears the prophet pull back: God means only to frighten them so they will repent.

sources.quote: אותה הכלה תהיה נבהלה כלומר תהיה בבהלה פתאום
sources.says: Radak says the destruction will come in a sudden rush.

sources.quote: אבל הנביא חוזר מדבריו ואומר אך נבהלה יעשה את כל יושבי הארץ, אין דעתו לכלות רק להבהיל אותם כדי שיעשו תשובה
sources.says: Malbim says the prophet takes back his words: God's aim is not to destroy them, only to frighten them into repenting.

2:1.headline: התקוששו can mean gather like straw, search yourselves, or straighten yourselves
2:1.body: The verb is built on קש, straw, so it can mean to gather together. Radak also reads it as searching out faults, and the sages read it as straightening yourself before others.

sources.quote: התחפשו מומיכם וחפשו מומים אחרים אחר כך ובערו אותם וכן ארז"ל מזה הפסוק קשט עצמך ואחר כך קשט אחרים
sources.says: Radak says the verb means searching out faults, first your own and then other people's, and he adds the sages' reading: straighten yourself first, then others.

sources.quote: קַשֵּׁט עַצְמְךָ וְאַחַר כָּךְ קַשֵּׁט אֲחֵרִים. עָשׂוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם לְשׁוֹן ׳הֶקֵּשׁ׳, אָדָם הַמַּשְׁוֶה עַצְמוֹ וּמְיַשֵּׁר דַּרְכּוֹ
sources.says: Rashi gives the sages' reading, straighten yourself and then others, and ties it to a word for making things level and straight.

sources.quote: התווכחו והוכיחו. ור' משה אמר: התקבצו וקבצו מגזרת מקושש קש שהוא לאסוף הקש
sources.says: Ibn Ezra gives two readings: argue and rebuke, or, from R. Moshe, gather and collect, like the verb for gathering straw.

2:1.headline: נכסף means longing in one reading and shame in another
2:1.body: Ibn Ezra takes it from longing, so this is a nation no one loves or wants. Radak's father heard shame in it, a nation that does not blush at what it does.

sources.quote: אינו אהוב ונחמד לגוים, מגזרת: נכספה וגם כלתה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the nation is one not loved or desired, and ties the word to the longing in "he longed and was spent".

sources.quote: אדוני אבי ז"ל כתב זה הגוי שאינו נכלם ולא יבוש ממעשיו מלשון רז"ל איכסיף באכסופי אפין
sources.says: Radak quotes his father: the nation does not feel shame at its deeds, reading the word from the sages' phrase for faces turning pale with shame.

2:4.headline: The name Ashdod (אשדוד) holds the word for plunder
2:4.body: The verse says Ashdod is driven out at noon. Radak says noon is named because ruin plunders at noon, and the name sounds like שד, plunder.

sources.quote: זכר צהרים לפי שהקטב ישוד בצהרים ואשדוד לשון שד והרי הוא כאלו הוא לשון נופל על הלשון
sources.says: Radak says noon is mentioned because ruin plunders at noon, and that אשדוד sounds like שד, a play of one word on another.

sources.quote: אַשְׁדּוֹד שְׁמָהּ, וּבַצָּהֳרַיִם אֲשֶׁר יָשֹׁד בָּהּ קֶטֶב יְגָרְשׁוּהָ וּתְהִי שְׁדוּדָה
sources.says: Rashi says its name is Ashdod, and when ruin plunders it at noon they will drive it out and it will be plundered.

2:5.headline: חבל: a measuring rope, then a strip of land, then a share
2:5.body: Land was measured with a rope, so חבל came to mean a region, here the coast. Later, in verse 7, Rashi reads it as a lot or share given to Judah.

sources.quote: וּלְשׁוֹן ׳חֶבֶל׳ – מִדַּת הַקַּרְקַע הִיא, שֶׁמּוֹדְדִין בְּחֶבֶל. כְּלוֹמַר הַסְּמוּכִים לַיָּם
sources.says: Rashi says חבל is a measure of ground, since land is measured with a rope, so it means the people next to the sea.

sources.quote: חֶבֶל זֶה לְשׁוֹן ׳גּוֹרָל׳ הוּא, וְכֵן תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן: ״וִיהֵי עַדְבָּא לִשְׁאָרָא דְבֵית יְהוּדָה
sources.says: Rashi says that in verse 7 חבל means a lot, and Jonathan translates it that way.

sources.quote: חלק כמו חבל נחלתו והוא ארץ פלשתים שהיא סמוכה לים
sources.says: Radak says חבל means a portion, like "the portion of his inheritance", and here it is the land by the sea.

2:5.headline: The Philistines' name כרתים sounds like "cut off"
2:5.body: Malbim hears the verb "to be cut off" in the name. Jonathan, quoted by Rashi, translates it as a people condemned to be destroyed.

sources.quote: הם הפלשתים שנקראו גוי כרתים (והלשון נופל על שיכרתו
sources.says: Malbim says the Philistines are called Kerethites, and the wording plays on "that they will be cut off".

sources.quote: תִּרְגֵּם יוֹנָתָן: ״עַמָּא דְמְחֻיָּבִין לְאִשְׁתְּצָאָה
sources.says: Rashi quotes Jonathan translating the name as a people condemned to be destroyed.

sources.quote: פלשתים יקראו כרתים כמ"ש אל נגב הכרתי ונאמר הכרתי את כרתים
sources.says: Radak says the Philistines are called Kerethites, as in "the south of the Kerethite" and "I will cut off the Kerethites".

2:6.headline: כרת may mean to dig, or to prepare a meal
2:6.body: Radak says the shepherds dig pits, from כרה, to dig. Rashi ties it to the great feast of 2 Kings 6:23, where the same root means preparing food.

sources.quote: נְוֵה עֲרַאי שֶׁיִּכְרוּ בָּהּ הָרוֹעִים לֶחֶם בַּבֹּקֶר. כְּרֹת לְשׁוֹן ״וַיִּכְרֶה לָהֶם כֵּרָה גְדוֹלָה
sources.says: Rashi says it is a shepherds' lodging where they will prepare bread in the morning, and links כרת to "he prepared a great feast" in 2 Kings 6:23.

sources.quote: מקום שיכרו שם הרעים להיות שם מקניהם נכלאים מן כי יכרה איש בור
sources.says: Radak says it is a place where shepherds dig to pen their flocks, from "if a man digs a pit".

sources.quote: וכרה היא הסעודה שיעשו הרועים ביחד לסימן על ברית השלום
sources.says: Malbim says כרה is the meal the shepherds make together as a sign of peace between them.

2:8.headline: גדופי is used only for insults against what is holy
2:8.body: The verse pairs it with חרפה, insult. Malbim says גידוף is only said of holy things, as in blaspheming God, so Ammon insulted Israel's Torah and holiness.

sources.quote: הגידוף הוא רק על דברים המקודשים, כמו את ה' הוא מגדף
sources.says: Malbim says גידוף is used only of holy things, like "he blasphemes the Lord".

sources.quote: ובני עמון גדפו תורתם וקדושתם
sources.says: Malbim says Ammon reviled Israel's Torah and holiness.

2:8.headline: ויגדילו על גבולם: took more land, or spoke big against Israel
2:8.body: Metzudat David gives two readings. They took Israel's land to enlarge their own border, or they spoke harsh, big words as Israel passed.

sources.quote: לקחו מאדמת ישראל להגדיל ולהוסיף על גבולם כמ״ש לבני עמון וגומר מדוע ירש מלכם את גד (ירמיהו מ״ט:א׳), או ר״ל כשעברו ישראל על גבולם דברו שם למולם דברים גדולים וקשים לבזותם
sources.says: Metzudat David says either they took Israel's land to enlarge their border, or they spoke big and harsh words to shame Israel as it crossed.

sources.quote: היו מגדילים פיהם בשחוק או לשונם לדבר בעברם על גבולם או פי' היו מגדילים פיהם על גבול ישראל
sources.says: Radak says they made their mouths big against Israel, in mockery or while passing the border.

sources.quote: וַיִּתְגָּאוּ עַל גְּבוּלָם
sources.says: Rashi says they grew proud over their border.

2:14.headline: Each commentator names a different part of the house for כפתור
2:14.body: Rashi says a knob at the top of the roof. Metzudat Zion says the lintel, because it is carved with knobs, and Ibn Ezra says the strongest part of the door.

sources.quote: פומל״ש שֶׁבְּרֹאשׁ הַגָּג
sources.says: Rashi says it is the pommel, a knob at the top of the roof.

sources.quote: כן יקרא המשקוף לפי שעושין בו ציורי כפתורים
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says the lintel is called this because it is carved with knob shapes.

sources.quote: הכפתור הוא החזק והקשה שבדלת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the כפתור is the strongest and hardest part of the door.

2:14.headline: ערה can mean uprooted or laid bare
2:14.body: Rashi reads it as uprooted, like "raze it, raze it". Ibn Ezra reads it as laid bare, so the ruin uncovers the cedar ceiling.

sources.quote: כִּי אֲרָזֶיהָ עִקֵּר וְשֵׁרַשׁ, כְּמוֹ ״עָרוּ עָרוּ
sources.says: Rashi says its cedars are rooted up, like "raze it, raze it".

sources.quote: כי החורב גילה הסיפון, כמו: וקיר ערה מגן
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says the ruin uncovered the cedar ceiling, like "Kir uncovered the shield".

3:1.headline: Morah: filthy, feared, or rebellious?
3:1.body: Rashi and Radak read מראה as filthy, like the bird's crop that is thrown away. Malbim reads it from יראה, fear: a city the nations were afraid of. Ibn Ezra also brings a view that it means rebellious.

sources.quote: מֹרְאָה – כְּמוֹ ״מֻרְאָתוֹ״
sources.says: Rashi says morah is like the bird's crop, mur'ato, in Leviticus.

sources.quote: וענינו מן ושמתיך כראי ענין טנוף ולכלוך
sources.says: Radak says it comes from 'I will make you like dung', meaning filth and dirt.

sources.quote: מוראה. מענין יראה
sources.says: Malbim says morah comes from the sense of fear.

sources.quote: ורבי ישועה אמר: מגזרת סורר ומורה
sources.says: Ibn Ezra cites Rabbi Yeshua that it comes from 'stubborn and rebellious'.

3:4.headline: Men of treachery, or lovers of unfaithful wives?
3:4.body: Radak reads בגדות as a plain noun, treacheries. Ibn Ezra and Malbim read it as women: the prophets were men who went with wives who betrayed their husbands.

sources.quote: אנשי בוגדות. שם בפלס הסוללות
sources.says: Radak says bogdot is a noun built like solelot, siege ramps.

sources.quote: והם אנשים לנשים בוגדות
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they are men belonging to treacherous women.

sources.quote: הם אנשים לנשים הבוגדות בבעליהן ומזנות עמהם
sources.says: Malbim says they are men of women who betray their husbands and sin with them.

3:4.headline: The priests 'robbed' the Torah
3:4.body: חמס usually means violence. Metzudat Zion says here it means taking away, as in Lamentations. Rashi says they did not teach the Torah to those who asked, and Ibn Ezra says they did not judge by it.

sources.quote: ענין הסרה כמו ויחמוס כגן שכו
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means removing, as in 'He stripped His booth like a garden'.

sources.quote: לֹא הוֹרוּ אוֹתָהּ לְשׁוֹאֲלֵיהֶם
sources.says: Rashi says they did not teach it to those who asked them.

sources.quote: חמסו תורת המשפט ולא דנו כדת
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says they did violence to the law and did not judge by it.

3:9.headline: A 'clear language': Hebrew, or pure belief?
3:9.body: Metzudat David says the clear language is Hebrew, the holy tongue, and Ibn Ezra brings the same from Rabbi Moshe. Radak and Malbim say it means speech with no other gods in it: everyone will call on the one God.

sources.quote: שידברו בלשון הקדש במקום הלשון שמדברים עכשיו
sources.says: Metzudat David says they will speak the holy tongue instead of the language they speak now.

sources.quote: בשפה ברורה הוא לשון הקודש, שבה לבדה נקרא השם הנכבד
sources.says: Ibn Ezra cites Rabbi Moshe that the clear language is the holy tongue, the only one in which God's name is called.

sources.quote: שלא יוציאו בשפתם אלהים אחרים אלא כולם יקראו בשם ה' זהו שפה ברורה
sources.says: Radak says they will not utter other gods with their lips, but all will call on the Lord, and that is the clear language.

sources.quote: ואז יקראו בשפה ברורה באחדות הבורא
sources.says: Malbim says they will then speak clearly of the oneness of the Creator.

3:12.headline: A poor people, or a humble one?
3:12.body: עני usually means poor. Radak reads it as ענו, humble, the opposite of the proud ones removed in the verse before. Malbim splits the pair: עני is humble in spirit, דל is poor in money.

sources.quote: הפך עליזי גאותך שזכר ופי' עני כמו עניו
sources.says: Radak says this is the opposite of the proud ones just mentioned, and ani means humble.

sources.quote: עני הוא שפל רוח ונגזר מפעל ענה שמורה הכנעה ומזה שם ענו, ודל הוא ברכוש
sources.says: Malbim says ani is lowly in spirit, from the root for humbling, while dal is poor in property.

sources.quote: עַם עַנְוְתָן וּמְקַבֵּל עֻלְבָּן
sources.says: Rashi says it is a humble people who accept insult.

3:15.headline: God removes your 'judgments': punishments, or unjust judges?
3:15.body: Rashi says משפטיך here means your punishments. Radak says it means the harsh rulings the nations passed on you in exile. The Targum and Malbim read it as the crooked judges among you.

sources.quote: מִשְׁפָּטַיִךְ. יִסּוּרֶיךְ
sources.says: Rashi says your judgments means your sufferings.

sources.quote: משפטי הגוים שהיו נותנים עליך בגלות
sources.says: Radak says it means the judgments the nations imposed on you in exile.

sources.quote: אַגְלֵי יְיָ דַיָנֵי שִׁקְרָא מִגַוִיךְ
sources.says: The Targum renders it 'the Lord has exiled the false judges from among you'.

sources.quote: שסרו השופטים ומשפטיהם המעוותים
sources.says: Malbim says the judges and their crooked rulings are removed.

3:18.headline: Nugei: the grieving, or the ones pushed out?
3:18.body: Radak and Ibn Ezra read נוגי from יגון, grief. Rashi reads it as 'removed', like taking dross from silver, and says the only root letter here is the ג.

sources.quote: מענין יגון מבנין נפעל כמו בתולותיה נוגות
sources.says: Radak says it comes from grief, as in 'her maidens are grieving'.

sources.quote: נוגי - בנין נפעל מגזרת יגון
sources.says: Ibn Ezra says nugei comes from the root for grief.

sources.quote: לְשׁוֹן ׳הוֹצָאָה׳, כְּמוֹ ״הָגוֹ סִיגִים״
sources.says: Rashi says it means removing, as in 'remove the dross'.

sources.quote: וְאֵין שֹׁרֶשׁ בַּתֵּבָה אֶלָּא הַגִּימֶ״ל לְבַדָּהּ
sources.says: Rashi says the only root letter in the word is the gimel.

3:18.headline: Cut off from the festivals, or grieving the long delay?
3:18.body: Rashi says these are people who were cut off because they did not keep Sabbaths and festivals. Radak says they grieved because the time of redemption was so long in coming. Malbim reads מועד from a slipping foot: those who fell away from the faith.

sources.quote: שֶׁלֹּא הָיוּ מְשַׁמְּרִים שַׁבָּתוֹת וְיָמִים טוֹבִים
sources.says: Rashi says they did not keep Sabbaths and festivals.

sources.quote: בנים שהיו נוגי' ממועד הגאולה שארך כל כך
sources.says: Radak says they were children who grieved because the set time of redemption took so long.

sources.quote: ממועד. מענין נכון למועדי רגל, ובא פה על מי שמט מאמונת ישראל
sources.says: Malbim says mimo'ed is from slipping feet, and here means one who slipped from the faith of Israel.

3:19.headline: God is 'doing' to your oppressors: crushing them
3:19.body: עשה usually means to do or make. Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as squeezing and crushing, as in Ezekiel. Rashi brings the Targum, 'making an end', and also links it to ועסותם, 'you will trample'.

sources.quote: כמו בעשות מצרים דדיך ענין הסחיטה והכתישה
sources.says: Radak says it is as in Ezekiel's 'when Egypt squeezed', meaning squeezing and crushing.

sources.quote: ענין כתישה ומעוך
sources.says: Metzudat Zion says it means crushing and pressing.

sources.quote: הָא אֲנָא עָבֵיד גְּמִירָא
sources.says: Rashi cites the Targum: 'I am making an end'.

sources.quote: כְּמוֹ ״וְעַסּוֹתֶם רְשָׁעִים״
sources.says: Rashi says it can be read like 'you will trample the wicked'.
